note: Starting points, not an inventory. Every organisation is different: take what fits, change the wording, and delete the rest. Scores are a first guess to argue with, not an answer.

items.name: Key personnel / single points of knowledge
Fraud monitoring and transaction scoring engine
In-country data centre and disaster recovery site

items.title: Business Email Compromise / Wire Fraud
items.description: Attackers impersonate executives or vendors to trick finance staff into redirecting a wire transfer, resulting in direct financial loss.

items.title: Core Banking or Trading System Outage
items.description: A failure or attack on core banking or trading systems halts customer transactions, triggering financial loss and regulatory scrutiny.

items.title: Cardholder Data Breach
items.description: Payment card data held or processed by the organisation is exposed, triggering PCI DSS non-compliance findings and card-scheme penalties.

items.title: Large-Scale Customer Account Takeover
items.description: Credential-stuffing attacks compromise customer accounts at scale, resulting in fraudulent transactions and reimbursement costs.

items.title: Insider Misuse of Financial Data
items.description: An employee with privileged access to financial systems misuses customer or market data for personal gain, including potential insider trading.

items.title: Gaps in Anti-Money-Laundering Screening
items.description: Weaknesses in transaction monitoring or customer screening let money laundering pass undetected, exposing the organisation to regulatory penalties and prosecution.

items.title: Abuse of Open Banking APIs
items.description: Poorly secured open-banking APIs are exploited to scrape customer data or perform unauthorized transactions.

items.title: Physical Skimming at ATMs or POS Terminals
items.description: Card-skimming devices installed on ATMs or point-of-sale terminals capture customer card data for later fraud.

items.title: Tampering with Financial Reporting Data
items.description: Financial records are altered without authorization, undermining the integrity of statutory financial reporting.

items.title: Regulatory Non-Compliance Fines
items.description: The organisation fails to meet financial-sector regulatory requirements, resulting in fines, sanctions or licence restrictions.

items.title: Synthetic Identity Fraud at Onboarding
items.description: Accounts are opened using fabricated identity details, or real details blended from more than one person, which pass basic verification. The fraud that follows is hard to trace back to any real victim.

items.title: Errors in Automated Credit or Trading Decision Models
items.description: Flaws or drift in automated credit-scoring or trading algorithms produce incorrect decisions, causing financial loss or unfair customer outcomes and regulatory scrutiny.

items.title: Unpatched critical vulnerability exploited
items.description: A known flaw in an internet-facing system is not patched inside the agreed window and is exploited before anyone notices it was outstanding.

items.title: Staff credentials taken by phishing
items.description: An employee enters their password and one-time code on a convincing fake login page, handing an attacker a legitimate session.

items.title: Supplier breach exposing customer data
items.description: A third party holding or processing your data is compromised, and your customers are affected by an incident that never touched your network.

items.title: Cloud storage or service left publicly accessible
items.description: A misconfiguration exposes a bucket, database or console to the internet, usually discovered by somebody outside the organisation.

items.title: Privileged administrator misuses their access
items.description: Someone with unrestricted rights reads, changes or removes what they should not, and without session recording nobody can prove what happened.

items.title: Leaver keeps access after departure
items.description: Accounts are not revoked when someone leaves, so a former employee or contractor still holds a working way in.

items.title: Malware spreads across a flat network
items.description: An infection on one endpoint reaches servers and other segments because the network is not divided, turning one machine into an estate-wide incident.

items.title: Vulnerable third-party library shipped to production
items.description: An open-source dependency with a known flaw is built into an application because nothing checks what the software is actually made of.

items.title: Sensitive data leaves through email or removable media
items.description: A member of staff sends or copies customer data out of the organisation, whether carelessly or deliberately.

items.title: Intrusion goes undetected for months
items.description: An attacker is inside the network but nothing raises an alarm, so the first notification comes from a regulator, a customer or the press.

items.title: Denial of service against online banking
items.description: A volumetric or application-layer attack makes the banking channel unreachable, which customers and the regulator experience as an outage regardless of whether any data was touched.

items.title: Disaster recovery fails when it is actually needed
items.description: Failover has been documented but never genuinely tested, and the recovery site does not come up when the primary is lost.

items.title: Expired certificate takes a service down
items.description: Nobody owns a certificate or is warned before it lapses, and a public service stops working for reasons that look like an attack.

items.title: An untested change breaks production
items.description: A change is applied without adequate testing or a way back, causing an outage. More incidents come from changes than from attackers.

items.title: Systems in use that nobody knows about
items.description: Departments buy or build their own tools, so data sits outside every control the organisation believes it has.

items.title: Cyber security has no clear owner or budget
items.description: Responsibility is spread across roles with no single accountable person and no funding, so nothing improves between assessments.

items.title: Risks are identified but never treated
items.description: A register exists and is presented, but decisions are not carried out, so the same findings appear year after year.

items.title: Unauthorised physical access to a data centre or branch
items.description: Someone reaches equipment or documents in person, through tailgating, a stale badge or an unescorted visit.

items.title: Systems built without reference to any security standard
items.description: Each project decides its own security, because there is no approved baseline to build against. The result is an estate where no two systems are protected the same way and nothing can be assessed as a whole.

items.title: Self-assessment overstates how mature you are
items.description: Scores are recorded from memory or optimism rather than evidence, so the programme looks compliant until an assessor asks to see the proof. The gap is discovered at the worst possible moment, by somebody else.

items.title: Known sector attack technique not acted on
items.description: Other banks are hit by a technique, the warning reaches the organisation, and nothing is checked or changed. The second victim had the same notice as the first and used it differently.

items.title: Security spending with no strategy behind it
items.description: Security projects are funded one at a time as problems arise, with no approved strategy or roadmap, so effort follows whatever is urgent and the organisation never reaches a defined target state.

items.title: New systems go live without a security review
items.description: Projects reach production without security requirements, a start-of-project risk assessment or an independent security review, and weaknesses are found only after customers are using the system.

items.title: Administrators and developers lack security skills for their roles
items.description: Staff who build and run critical systems have never had role-specific security training, leading to insecure configuration and code that general awareness training does not prevent.

items.title: Cyber security audits that are not independent or not planned
items.description: Security is audited irregularly, or by people who run the controls being audited, so weaknesses go unreported until SAMA or an attacker finds them.

items.title: Business data on unmanaged personal phones
items.description: Staff read customer or business information on their own phones with no device management or separation of business data, so a lost, stolen or jailbroken phone exposes it.

items.title: Customer data recovered from disposed equipment
items.description: Disks, laptops or printers leave the organisation without secure wiping or destruction, or through a disposal contractor nobody checks, and customer data is later recovered from them.

items.title: Loss of SARIE settlement connectivity
items.description: The connection to the national settlement system fails or is disrupted, stopping interbank transfers and leaving customer payments unsettled.

items.title: Failure to notify SAMA immediately of a serious incident
items.description: A medium or high incident is not reported to SAMA IT Risk Supervision immediately, as the framework requires, turning an incident into a compliance breach on top of it.

items.title: Customer data held outside Saudi Arabia
items.description: A cloud service or supplier stores or processes regulated data outside the Kingdom, breaching data residency obligations.

items.title: Material outsourcing without prior SAMA approval
items.description: A significant service is outsourced before the regulator has approved the arrangement, which is a finding regardless of how well the supplier performs.

items.title: SWIFT customer security controls not met at attestation
items.description: Mandatory controls are found missing at the annual attestation, risking counterparty confidence as well as regulatory attention.

items.title: Compromise of payment cryptographic keys
items.description: Keys held for card or payment operations are exposed through weak handling or a compromised module, putting every transaction signed with them in doubt.

items.title: Concentration on a single cloud provider
items.description: Critical services depend on one provider or one region, so an outage or a contractual dispute takes down more than any single system.

items.title: Mada or scheme compliance lapse
items.description: Scheme rules change or an obligation is missed, risking penalties or suspension from the national card scheme.

items.title: Ransomware reaching backup copies
items.description: An attacker with administrative access deletes or encrypts the backups as well as the live systems, removing the one route back.

items.title: Branch or ATM cash-out attack
items.description: Attackers manipulate card or ATM systems to dispense cash beyond account balances, usually across many machines in a short window.
